newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwandan police seek killers of judge.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan police seek killers of judge.

text.p: The body of a top Rwandan judge was taken to his village for burial on Sunday -- the latest victim of a wave of killings in his country. Police said they had not yet tracked down his killers.

Vincent Nzezabaganwa, head of the state council court and vice-president of the Rwandan supreme court, was gunned down at his Kigali home on Friday night by men wearing uniform. Three other men, who were visiting him, were also killed.
Nzezabaganwa's widow and five children cried quietly as they held an all-night vigil over his coffin in their modest Kigali home before the burial on Sunday.
The coffin was draped in a Rwandan flag for the 20 km (12 miles) journey to the village north of Kigali.
"He had enemies who were jealous, but we cannot say who was responsible," his widow, Leonice, told Reuters. "Times are like that.
"The killers were in military uniform, but we cannot be sure who they were."

An upsurge of violence in the last two months has claimed hundreds of lives, including a Canadian Roman Catholic priest and several other expatriates, but has largely been restricted to countryside areas away from the capital.
The killing of four United Nations monitors in southern Rwanda early this month prompted the U.N. to order its staff to remain in Kigali.
But Nzezabaganwa's murder showed that he was clearly targeted, and that the killers were able to operate in the capital.
"We have so far been unable to arrest anyone, but the investigation is ongoing," a police spokesman said.

Nzezabaganwa, a Hutu, was not directly involved in the trials of alleged perpetrators of the genocide in which up to 800,000 Tutsis and allied Hutus were slaughtered in 1994 after the death in a plane crash of president Juvenal Habyarimana, a Hutu.
Over 90,000 Rwandans, mostly Hutus, are now awaiting trial in connection with the genocide. Eleven have so far been sentenced to death, and are awaiting the outcome of their appeals.
Officials of the government and army have blamed the recent murders on Hutu extremists and elements of the former Hutu armed forces who fled the country, fearing retribution, after the 1994 genocide.
More than a million Hutus who fled as refugees in 1994 have returned since last November, and have been absorbed into the Rwandan countryside.
Rwandan radio on Saturday said measures would be taken to ensure security in Kigali and other areas.
During January, U.N. monitors recorded 201 killings -- including 30 blamed on anti-government insurgents.
